title: The Multimodal Future of Education: Stefania Druga

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk centers on how children and families perceive, trust, and collaborate with AI in educational contexts, fitting human-factors and UX inclusion criteria. The entire presentation focuses on transforming K-12 education through multimodal AI tools and learning activities. The talk presents longitudinal research findings alongside working open-source demos deployed in schools and homes across multiple US states. Content is accessible to practitioners while incorporating research methodology and longitudinal study findings. The presentation combines slides with live Gemini API demonstrations interpreting hand-drawn inputs for science and math learning. Claims are supported by longitudinal studies and quantitative statistics, supplemented by live demos and informal classroom observations.

summary: Stefania Druga opens by framing education as needing a wakeup call: only 70% of 10-year-olds can read and understand a simple story, and 60% of children and teenagers fell behind in math and reading during COVID. 70% of generative AI users are Gen Z, and students already prefer AI tools over human tutors. She has researched children's interactions with AI since 2015, finding that perception of AI intelligence changes with age — younger kids (4-6.5) are skeptical of voice assistants, while older kids believe devices like Alexa are smarter than they are. To cultivate AI literacy, she built Cognimates in 2016, an open-source platform extending Scratch that lets kids train custom image and text models, program smart home devices, and build games. A longitudinal study in public and private schools showed that after learning how AI works through tinkering, kids became significantly more skeptical of AI's intelligence, engaging in the scientific process of forming and testing hypotheses. She explores family co-creation with AI programming co-pilots across 10 U.S. states, finding families value idea generation, code elaboration, and creative coding identity support, while noting limitations like distraction and inability to scaffold complex concepts or mediate sibling conflicts. She created the first benchmark for math misconceptions with Nancy Otodo. Live Gemini API demos interpret hand-drawn diagrams for science (a scale with weights, water and CO2 mixing, Earth hit by the moon) and math problems. In the final segment, she continues demos where AI responds to hand-drawn content by asking questions back rather than giving answers, encouraging curiosity — identifying a flag (Jordan), asking about an apple's smell, and solving a system of equations (2x + 7 = 2) step by step. She reveals the demo code is open source, under 100 lines, requiring only a free API key, and urges the audience to think beyond chatbot interfaces toward tinkerer-driven approaches that put tools in young people's hands.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Education Crisis and the First AI Generation
sections.summary: Stefania frames education as needing a wakeup call, citing literacy gaps (only 70% of 10-year-olds can read), COVID learning losses (60% behind in math and reading), and the fact that 70% of generative AI users are Gen Z. Students already prefer AI tools over human tutors.

sections.title: Children's Perception of AI and Voice Assistants
sections.summary: Research since 2015 shows younger kids (4-6.5) are skeptical of voice assistants' intelligence while older school-age kids believe devices like Alexa are smarter than themselves. These perceptions shape their queries, trust, and mental models of AI.

sections.title: Cognimates Platform and Custom Model Training
sections.summary: Cognimates (2016) extends Scratch, enabling kids to program smart devices, train custom image and text models, and build AI-powered games. Examples include unicorn-vs-narwhal classification, food detection, rock-paper-scissors, and a Shakespeare-talking robot. Used in 30+ languages worldwide.

sections.title: Evaluation Results: Increased Skepticism Through Tinkering
sections.summary: A longitudinal study in public and private schools found that after learning to train models and program smart devices, children became significantly more skeptical of AI's intelligence. By tinkering and testing hypotheses, kids engaged in the scientific process, transforming from passive users to critical creators. Includes parent and teacher perspectives.

sections.title: Family Co-Creation and AI Programming Co-Pilot Study
sections.summary: Study with families across 10 US states explored designing an AI co-pilot for programming. Families valued idea generation, code elaboration, creative coding identity support, and family joint engagement through a third-party moderator. Limitations included distraction, inability to handle sibling conflicts, and difficulty scaffolding complex concepts. Top generative AI models were benchmarked for Scratch programming support.

sections.title: Multimodal AI Vision and Live Gemini API Demos
sections.summary: Stefania envisions multimodal AI as creative sidekick, learning companion, and coach across games, physics simulations, and math. She created the first math misconceptions benchmark for K-12. Live demos with Gemini API interpret hand-drawn diagrams: a scale with weights, water and CO2 mixing, Earth hit by the moon, and a math expression solver.

sections.title: Continued Demos: Curiosity-Driven Questioning, System of Equations, and Open-Source Call to Action
sections.summary: Stefania continues live demos where Gemini API responds to hand-drawn inputs by asking questions back rather than giving answers, encouraging curiosity. Demos include identifying a flag (Jordan) by asking about colors and star shape, asking what an apple smells like, and solving a system of equations (2x + 7 = 2) step by step with user-guided operations. She reveals the demo code is open source, under 100 lines, requiring only a free API key, and urges the audience to think beyond chatbot interfaces toward tinkerer-driven approaches that put AI tools in the hands of young people. She shares a QR link to her research website.
